There are two paths in to the NSA. The first is military. Join a uniformed service and get into the intelligence career fields that have to do with signals and electronic systems security. It takes the highest scores on ASVAB to qualify for these fields. They will begin background investigations that will take a year or more. If you have any drug offenses, criminal convictions, or financial problems, that could be a problem. Bad credit or bankruptcy can prevent you from getting a security clearance. The investigation will know every piece of dirt on you. It is extensive and they dig deep. Yes they will talk to old girlfriends, people who are only remotely acquainted with you, old employers, school teachers, etc. They will want to know anything with which a foreign adversary might be able to blackmail you. If you are married or living with someone, they will also do a background check on that person also. Your spouse can keep you from getting a clearance if he/she has bad checks, criminal convictions, was born in certain foreign countries, etc.

While the investigation is going on, you will go to basic training and begin technical training after basic is done. The technical training has at least two phases. The first often involves a year at the Defense Language Institute Foreign Language Center where you will learn a language. DLI is one of the hardest schools you will attend in your life. Here's kind of how it works. You are in class eight hours day roughly. The first day, you get a list of vocabulary to memorize and a basic grammar lesson. There will be a test the next day. Depending on the service (I was in the Air Force), the passing grade is usually an 80%. If you pass the test, you get another lesson with more words, with another test the next day. Every single day, you are tested. Get less than an 80 on two tests in a row and you will flunk out and they will assign you to another career field, like a cook, infantry, mechanic, etc. By the end of the year, you will think nothing of getting a vocabulary list with 300 new words on it and having to take a test on it the next day, complete with grammar, spelling, etc. It is grueling, but you will adapt to it.

The second phase involves training in the basics of intelligence operations, which covers the technical and administrative parts of the career. Once you are assigned to a base (or an NSA site like Fort Meade), you will undergo several months of additional training. Basically, from the time you enter basic training to the time you actually become a qualified operations tech, you will have been in the service about two years. All of this will happen before you begin to work live missions. That's why the re-enlistment bonuses are so high, because it's not cost-effective to give you all that training and then have you get out 18 months later. They want you for at least one more enlistment to make it worth the investment into your training. If you can get a bachelor's degree while you are in, you can go to work for NSA when you retire or separate. Your clearance is your biggest asset. It costs $60,000 to $80,000 to do the clearance from scratch.

If you don't go the military route, you can get recruited from college. The same personal standards apply regarding drug use, criminal backgrounds, finances, etc. In college applicants they are looking for mathematicians (NSA hires more mathematicians than anywhere else in the world), computer science and security, and foreign languages (particularly any target languages of nations hostile to the US) like Farsi, Arabic, Pushtun, as well as Chinese, Russian, etc. You will undergo a similar training regime that will take a couple of years, depending on the field you are in.

If and when you leave the service or NSA, you will sign more nondisclosure agreements that you can imagine. If you publish a paper or a book on anything remotely related to your intelligence target area, it will have to be reviewed by NSA before you publish (which is why I majored in American history instead.) You may end up with travel restrictions that will last the rest of your life. You might not be allowed to fly in a commercial airliner over certain countries. Contacts with people from certain countries might need to be reported for as long as you live.

It can be a rewarding career field for patriotic people who are capable of some serious, devoted work. Keep in mind that, everyone you work with went to the same process and they are prime, grade-A prima donnas, just like you. It's like being in the tops of your class in law school. The people who make it are the best of the best and they know it. Humility is not a trait the process cultivates. When you are the one writing a report that is going to be on the desks of the National Security Council in ten minutes, you aren't going to be lacking in confidence. For that reason, the career field is extraordinarily competitive and almost everyone you work with can be an asshole (me included).
